name: Jessner peel

lead: The Jessner peel is a light chemical peel made from resorcinol, salicylic acid and lactic acid. It is used for fine lines, acne marks, uneven pigment and texture, and sometimes as a first layer before a deeper TCA peel, for smoother, clearer, more even skin.

The acids cause controlled superficial injury, after which the outer skin layers shed and renew. Specific research includes a 2021 comparative study in Indian women with melasma comparing a 35% glycolic acid peel with a Jessner peel as add-ons to a triple topical combination. Dermatologists also often choose lighter peels like Jessner for darker skin.

paras: It is a clinic peel, often done as a series, and it is commonly used to precede retinoic acid peels or the Jessner's + TCA combination.
Reported effects of peels include stinging, redness, dryness, photosensitivity and, less often, pigment change or scarring. Pigment complications are a recognised concern in darker skin.

chain: Acid mix sheds top skin layer
angle.text: It is a superficial peel used for fine lines, acne marks and uneven pigment, and to prime skin before deeper TCA or retinoic peels. The acid mix sheds the top skin layer so smoother, more even skin renews beneath.

lead: The Jessner peel is a superficial chemical peel based on Jessner's solution, a mixture of resorcinol, salicylic acid and lactic acid. Chemical peels are procedures in which an acid or other agent is applied to the skin to cause controlled injury, after which the skin sheds and renews itself; the general category is described as being used for fine lines, acne scarring and uneven pigmentation.[1] Retinoic acid peels are described as commonly being preceded by a Jessner peel.[1]

In dermatology literature the Jessner solution is also used as a pre-treatment step before a medium-depth trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel, a combination known as the Jessner's + TCA peel. Authors of a 2017 paper on TCA technique noted that physicians often choose lighter peels, such as glycolic acid or Jessner peels, and various lasers for patients with darker skin out of concern about pigmentary complications from deeper peels.[2]

Published human research specific to the Jessner peel is limited. A 2021 comparative study in Indian women with melasma compared a 35% glycolic acid peel with a Jessner peel as add-ons to a triple topical combination.[3]

Jessner's solution is named after Max Jessner, according to Wikipedia, and is used alone for light resurfacing or as a first step in combination peels.[1] Chemical peeling as a field traces to the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra in the second half of the 19th century, with phenol-croton oil peels entering mainstream practice in the 1960s.[1]

Melasma, acne, acne scars (as priming), uneven pigment

paras: The Jessner peel is generally classed among light-depth chemical peels. Light peels, as a group, are described as treating fine wrinkles, uneven pigmentation and acne, with side effects including stinging, redness, irritation and dryness.[1] Salicylic acid, one of its components, is a beta hydroxy acid described as oil-soluble and used in acne treatment.[1]

In some medium-depth protocols, a Jessner application is used first and TCA applied afterwards. A 1989 report described this Jessner's + TCA approach as a medium-depth peel used for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses and wrinkles.

Wikipedia notes retinoic acid peels are usually preceded by a Jessner's peel applied right beforehand, which opens the skin so the retinoic acid can penetrate deeper.[1] Depth ranges from AHA and BHA peels at the light end, to TCA peels at medium depth, to phenol peels historically at the deep end.[1] Professional peels are typically done by certified dermatologists or licensed estheticians, and medium-depth peels by a medical provider.[1]

Chemical peels in general are associated with photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, and in some cases scarring; deeper peels carry more risk.[1] Concern about pigmentary complications in darker skin is the reason some clinicians reported favouring lighter peels such as the Jessner peel over deeper ones.[2]

Wikipedia says deeper peels bring more complications, and that both professional peels and low-concentration home kits can cause skin injury and scarring; light AHA peels may cause stinging, redness and dryness.[1] A modified Jessner's series for Nevus of Ota notes that repetitive chemical peeling can cause irritation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[4] A 2021 study examined the safety of superficial chemical peels in patients on oral isotretinoin, a combination that is not currently recommended because of risks such as dryness, erythema, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and scarring.[5]

A 2021 study from Baroda Medical College, India, enrolled 60 women with melasma and compared a 35% glycolic acid peel with a Jessner peel, each added to a triple combination cream of hydroquinone, tretinoin and fluocinolone acetonide.[3] A later registered trial listed on ClinicalTrials.gov compared Jessner's solution with TCA for melasma in 19 participants (completed, Phase 4, start 2008). Jessner's solution has also been studied as a priming step in combination with TCA in the 1989 and 1995 dermatology papers.

A 2014 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study of 52 melasma patients compared ten sessions of low-fluence 1,064 nm Q-switched Nd:YAG laser plus a placebo peel against laser plus Jessner's solution at two-week intervals. At 8 weeks the mean MASI score fell from 8.98 to 7.13 in the Jessner group versus 8.68 to 8.60 with placebo (p<0.001), but at 20 weeks there was no significant difference in MASI, self-assessment or physician global assessment.[6]

A 2015 study of 50 patients with acne scars compared a modified Jessner's peel followed by 20% TCA against 20% TCA alone (25 per group). Marked improvement was seen in 60 percent of the combination group versus 28 percent with TCA alone, though the difference was not statistically significant.[7]

A 2021 prospective comparative study in Alexandria of 40 Egyptian women with melasma compared a single session of low-power fractional CO2 laser followed by Jessner's peel (up to six sessions) with Jessner's alone; both groups improved significantly on the modified MASI with no difference between them.[8] A 2020 case series of seven Nevus of Ota patients treated with Q-switched laser plus modified Jessner's peel for eight sessions reported more than 50 percent pigment reduction in 85.7 percent of patients.[4] A 2022 case report described treatment of hyperpigmented discoid lupus erythematosus with a Jessner's peel.[9]
The Jessner peel is listed in the wiki as a skin-resurfacing procedure within the hardmaxxing category. No forum material on it was collected for this entry.
